sessions.title: The story of salvation: creation, fall, and redemption
sessions.summary: The whole Bible in three words: Creation, Fall, Redemption. God made us one family, sin broke it, and Jesus gathers us home.

sources.title: Genesis 12:1-3 and 22:15-18: God's promises to Abraham
Pope Benedict XVI, homily at the start of his pontificate (2005)

sessions.ref: Symbolon Part 1: Knowing the Faith · Session 4
lesson: Every good story has a beginning, a crisis and a rescue. The Bible is the greatest of them, and it is true: it is the story of God and of us. Its shape fits in three words: Creation, Fall and Redemption. Once you see this shape, every part of Scripture finds its place.

Your Symbolon handout borrows a famous movie title for it: the greatest story ever told. This story, which we profess in the Creed, tells us that life has a purpose and that our own lives have a reason. We are not just spectators watching time go by. From the moment our first parents rebelled, through the Death and Resurrection of Jesus, God has been writing his plan of salvation. Each of us has a God-given role to play in it. If we refuse his loving invitation, the whole world is poorer, because God's story of love is not complete without each one of us.
[[art:Michelangelo - Creation of Adam (cropped).jpg|Michelangelo, The Creation of Adam (about 1512), Sistine Chapel, Vatican]]
[[figure:salvation]]
[[figure:ladder]]
## Creation: made for love

God is perfectly happy in himself. He did not need us. He made us freely, out of sheer goodness, so that we could share his own blessed life (Catechism 1). We were made to know him, to love him and to live with him forever.
> Each of us is the result of a thought of God. Each of us is willed, each of us is loved, each of us is necessary. — Pope Benedict XVI

In the beginning everything was in harmony: the first man and woman were at peace with God, with each other, with themselves and with creation (Catechism 374-376). Think of two lines: a vertical line joining us to God, and a horizontal line joining us to one another. In creation both were whole. Adam and Eve were one united human family, and that unity reflected the unity of God himself (Catechism 376).
## The Fall: love refused

God gave Adam and Eve real freedom, because love that is forced is not love. Tempted by the devil, they stopped trusting God and chose themselves instead of him (Catechism 396-398). They refused the self-giving love they were made for.

Both lines broke at once. The vertical bond with God was cut, and the horizontal bond between people cracked too. Even the harmony between man and woman was broken (Catechism 396): Adam blames Eve, Cain kills Abel, and the family of God scatters into a broken human family (Catechism 400). Sin also brought death into the world. The Church calls this wound original sin.
- Original sin: not a sin we committed, but a wounded human nature we inherited. We are born without the holiness and friendship with God that we were meant to have (Catechism 404-405).
- Concupiscence: the pull toward sin that remains even after Baptism washes original sin away. It is not itself a sin, but it makes the good harder to choose (Catechism 405, 1264).
## Redemption: God comes to rescue
God did not give up on us. Right after the Fall he promised a Saviour (Genesis 3:15). Then, step by step, through covenants, he began gathering his scattered family again.
Your class chart draws it as a rising line. God had a plan to restore humanity to himself and to each other through certain leaders, and each covenant made his family bigger:
- Adam and Eve: a couple.
- Noah: one family.
- Abraham: one tribe.
- Moses: one nation.
- David: one kingdom.
- Jesus: one universal, Catholic Church, the whole family of God.
God made three great promises to Abraham, and the rest of the Old Testament shows him keeping them:
- A great nation: his descendants would become a great nation. Fulfilled when God, through Moses, freed the Israelites from slavery in Egypt and made them his people at Sinai.
- A kingdom: fulfilled when King David expanded Israel's borders and it became a kingdom, and God promised that David's throne would last forever.
- A worldwide blessing: God would send the Messiah to gather all the nations back. Fulfilled in Jesus, the Son of David, who opens God's family to the whole world in the new and everlasting covenant.

In Jesus all three promises meet. The Son of God became man to die for our sins, offering on our behalf the perfect gift of love that restores us to the Father and to each other, making us one family of God (Catechism 457-460). He paid the debt of sin we could not pay and opened the door to eternal life. And he sent the Holy Spirit to fill us with his very life.
## The Church: God's family gathered

Jesus did not come to save us only one by one, as scattered individuals. He founded the universal, Catholic Church to gather the broken human family into the united family of God, a sign and instrument of our union with God and with each other (Catechism 775-776, 830). That is what "catholic" means: universal, sent to everyone (Catechism 830-831).

The Church, the renewed family of God, has three tasks: to proclaim the Gospel, to baptize, and to make disciples of all humanity (Matthew 28:19-20; Catechism 849). After Jesus ascended into heaven, the apostles carried on these three things, and the Church will keep doing them until the end of time, when Jesus comes back to judge the living and the dead. Through his teaching and the sacraments, the Church hands on the graces Jesus won on the Cross, so that we can live like Christ on earth and with him forever in heaven (Catechism 774-776).
## Where we fit in the story

This story is still being written, and we all have a part to play in God's plan of salvation. Every day we are called to choose between good and evil. Jesus calls us toward his love and a life of virtue, and he wants each of us to help spread his love to everyone we meet.

Satan is the chief enemy of everything good. He invites people to live for the world and a life of sin. You either walk toward the light of Christ, or toward the darkness and despair of the evil one. The way out is simple, though not always easy: turn toward the light of Christ, again and again. Each small choice for God is a step back into the family we were made for.

deeper.title: Why the story matters
deeper.text:
Without Creation, we would not know we are loved and made on purpose. Without the Fall, we could not explain why the world, and our own hearts, are so mixed up. Without Redemption, there would be no hope.

People sometimes call the Bible's story the greatest story ever told. It is better than a story, because it is true: God wrote himself into history to bring his children home.

- Catholic: from the Greek kath' holou, "according to the whole": the Church is for every people, place and time (Catechism 830-831).

- Redemption: buying back. Jesus paid the price of our freedom with his own life (Mark 10:45).

sessions.reflection: Where do you see the "broken lines" in your own life, with God or with the people around you? What is one small step toward the light this week?

sessions.title: Who is Jesus?
sessions.summary: Jesus is truly God and truly man: one divine Person with two natures. The Church guarded this truth against every distortion, because our salvation depends on it.

sources.title: John 14:1-14: the way, the truth and the life
Hebrews 1:1-4: God has spoken through his Son
Pope St. John Paul II, World Youth Day vigil, Rome (2000)

sessions.ref: Symbolon Part 1: Knowing the Faith · Session 5
lesson: > It is Jesus that you seek when you dream of happiness; he is waiting for you when nothing else you find satisfies you. — Pope St. John Paul II, World Youth Day 2000
[[art:Spas vsederzhitel sinay.jpg|Christ Pantocrator (6th century), St. Catherine's Monastery, Sinai: one face, truly God and truly man]]

The rest of St. John Paul II's words to young people in Rome (August 19, 2000), in short: Jesus is the beauty that attracts you. He is the one who stirs up in you a thirst for fullness that will not let you settle for compromise. He urges you to take off the masks of a false life, and he reads in your heart the most genuine choices you want to make, the ones others try to stifle.

Every person eventually has to answer the question Jesus asked his disciples: "Who do you say that I am?" (Matthew 16:15). Christianity is not first a set of rules or ideas. It is a relationship with a Person.
## God's final Word

For centuries God spoke to his people in many ways through the prophets. In Jesus he spoke his whole Word at once (Hebrews 1:1-2). Christ, the Son of God made man, is the Father's one, perfect and unsurpassable Word; there will be no other word than this one. St. John of the Cross put it beautifully: in giving us his Son, God told us everything, and he has nothing more to say. What he once said in parts through the prophets, he has now said all at once. So anyone who still asks God for some new vision or revelation would be acting foolishly, and even offending him, by not fixing their eyes entirely on Christ (Catechism 65).

- No new public revelation: Christ's covenant is the new and definitive one, and it will never pass away. We do not wait for a new gospel before Jesus comes again in glory. Yet Revelation has not been made completely explicit, so the Church spends the centuries grasping more fully what Jesus has already given (Catechism 66).

- Private revelations: some, like Fatima or Lourdes, are approved by the Church. They do not belong to the deposit of faith, and they cannot improve or complete what Christ revealed; they help people live it more fully in a certain time. Guided by the Magisterium, the sense of the faithful (sensus fidelium) can tell which of them are an authentic call of Christ or his saints. No Catholic is required to believe them (Catechism 67).

- For everyone: God wants all people to be saved and to come to know the truth, which is Christ Jesus (1 Timothy 2:4). So Christ must be proclaimed to every nation and every person, and God arranged for what he revealed to be handed on whole, to all generations, to the ends of the earth (Catechism 74).
## True God and true man

At the time God chose, the only Son of the Father, the eternal Word and perfect Image of the Father, became flesh without losing his divine nature (Catechism 479). He did not just look human. He became truly one of us while remaining truly God. This is the Incarnation: God taking on flesh (Catechism 464). Because he is true God and true man in one divine Person, he is the one and only mediator between God and humanity (Catechism 480).
[[figure:natures]]

Jesus is one Person, the eternal Son, with two natures, one divine and one human. They are united without being mixed together and without being split apart (Catechism 481). As man he had a real body, a human soul, a human mind that learned, and a human will. His human mind and will were perfectly in tune with, and freely obedient to, the divine mind and will he shares with the Father and the Holy Spirit (Catechism 470-475, 482). He got tired, wept, and felt joy and fear. He is like us in all things but sin (Hebrews 4:15). The Incarnation is the mystery of this wonderful union of the divine and human natures in the one Person of the Word (Catechism 483).
## Why the Church guarded every word

In the first centuries, Christians worked hard to protect and explain the core truth of the Incarnation: that Jesus Christ is one divine Person with two natures. Thinkers who tried to understand it often fell into errors, called heresies. Each one trimmed away part of the mystery and ended up with a Jesus who could not save us. They fall into three groups. The Church's great councils answered them, and that is where the precise words of our Creed come from.
### 1. Heresies that denied or shrank his divine nature

- Arianism (4th century): taught by Arius. The Son of God was not eternal but created, the highest and first of God's creatures, yet not God himself. The first ecumenical council, Nicaea (325), condemned it and confessed that the Son is "begotten, not made, consubstantial with the Father" (Catechism 465).
- Adoptionism (3rd century): Jesus was born purely human and was "adopted" by God as his Son, at his baptism or his Resurrection, because of his exceptional holiness and obedience.
### 2. Heresies that denied or shrank his human nature

- Docetism and Gnosticism (1st-2nd centuries): from the Greek dokein, "to seem" or "to appear." Jesus was purely divine and only appeared to have a body, to eat, to suffer and to die on the Cross. The Gnostics saw physical matter as evil, so they rejected the idea that God could take on real flesh (Catechism 465).

- Apollinarianism (4th century): Jesus had a real human body and a living soul, but no human mind; the divine Word took its place. The Church rejected this, because a human being without a human mind is not fully human.

- Monophysitism (5th century): after the Incarnation, Christ's human nature was swallowed up by his divine nature, like a drop of water in the sea. The Council of Chalcedon (451) answered that Christ has two complete natures, divine and human, without confusion or change, in one Person (Catechism 467).
### 3. A heresy that split the union of the two natures

- Nestorianism (5th century): taught by Nestorius, Patriarch of Constantinople. Jesus was really two persons, a human one and a divine one, joined only by love or purpose. So Nestorius refused to call Mary Theotokos, Mother of God, saying she was only the mother of the human person. The Council of Ephesus (431) condemned this, declaring that the divine Word united a human nature to himself in his one divine Person (the hypostasis), which makes Mary truly the Mother of God (Catechism 466).
## Why it matters

This is not word-games. The truth about who Jesus is is tied to our salvation, which is why the Church still fights false teachings today. If Jesus were not fully God, he would have no power to forgive sins, defeat death and restore humanity's union with God. If he were not fully man, he could not fully enter our human condition, including suffering on our behalf, to heal and restore our human nature. The early Church Fathers summed it up: what was not taken up by Christ was not redeemed.
## Lord, liar, or something worse?

Jesus forgave sins, claimed to be one with the Father, and accepted worship. C.S. Lewis, an Oxford professor, a famous 20th-century defender of the Christian faith and the author of The Chronicles of Narnia, warned against the "really foolish thing" people say: that they accept Jesus as a great moral teacher but not his claim to be God. A mere man who said what Jesus said would not be a great teacher. He would be a lunatic, on the level of a man who says he is a poached egg, or else the Devil of Hell. You must choose: either he was, and is, the Son of God, or a madman or something worse. You can dismiss him as a fool, reject him as a demon, or fall at his feet and call him Lord and God. But the polite middle option of a great human teacher, Lewis says, "He has not left that open to us. He did not intend to."
Jesus answers the question himself: "I am the way and the truth and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me" (John 14:6).
## Meeting him

Archbishop Fulton Sheen, the much-loved TV bishop, made an hour of prayer before the Blessed Sacrament every day of his priesthood. He said that neither knowing theology nor doing good works is enough, on its own, to keep us in love with Christ; both must come from a personal encounter with him. Insight into God comes not only from between the two covers of a book, "but from two bent knees before an altar." He called the Holy Hour an oxygen tank that revives the breath of the Holy Spirit in the middle of the world's stale air. Knowing about Jesus is a start; the goal is to know him, personally, in prayer, Scripture and the sacraments.

deeper.title: Words the Church uses for Jesus
deeper.text:
- Incarnation: from the Latin for "in the flesh." The Son of God became man in the womb of the Virgin Mary (John 1:14).

- Hypostatic union: the theologian's name for two natures united in one divine Person.

- Consubstantial: of the same substance. We say it in the Creed: the Son is God in exactly the same way the Father is.

- Theotokos: Greek for God-bearer. Calling Mary the Mother of God is really a statement about who Jesus is.

- Christ: Greek for Messiah, "the anointed one." It is a title, not a surname.

sessions.reflection: Jesus asks you, not just the apostles: "Who do you say that I am?" How would you answer today? Try spending fifteen quiet minutes with him this week, in a church if you can.

sessions.title: The Paschal Mystery
sessions.summary: The Paschal Mystery is Jesus' passion, death, resurrection and ascension: how he restored our friendship with God, and how he invites us to share in it.

sources.title: 1 Peter 3:18-19 and 4:6: preaching to the dead

sessions.ref: Symbolon Part 1: Knowing the Faith · Session 6
lesson: The Paschal Mystery is the mystery of Jesus' death and resurrection. It is the centre of the whole faith: everything before it points toward it, and everything after it flows from it.
[[art:Cristo crucificado.jpg|Diego Velázquez, Christ Crucified (about 1632), Prado Museum, Madrid]]
## The cross was shocking

Perhaps the cross has become almost too familiar. We see crosses everywhere, on walls, steeples and necklaces, so it is easy to forget that in the ancient world it was a horrifying image. Crucifixion was the cruelest and most shameful execution Rome had. A Roman wearing a cross around his neck as jewellery would have seemed as bizarre and shocking to his neighbours as someone today wearing a little electric chair. Yet the cross is the main symbol of our faith, because through Jesus' death on that instrument of torture he gave us the gift of salvation and eternal life (Symbolon).
## Why "Paschal"?

Pascha is the Greek form of the Hebrew word for Passover. At the first Passover the blood of a lamb saved Israel's firstborn, and God led his people out of slavery in Egypt. Jesus is the new Passover Lamb (1 Corinthians 5:7). By his passion, death, resurrection and ascension, he leads us out of slavery to sin and death (Catechism 571).

We proclaim this at every Mass: "We proclaim your Death, O Lord, and profess your Resurrection until you come again." Beneath it all is one simple reality: Jesus gave himself completely, in love, to the Father on our behalf, to restore our relationship with God. And by his death on the cross, Jesus also shows us that we are called to the same sacrificial love, the love that leads to true happiness here on earth and eternal joy in the next life.
## Why did Jesus die for our sins?
[[figure:bridge]]
- A real gap between God and humanity: because of sin there was a true break between God the Father and man. Sin is not a small mistake. It broke our friendship with God, the very source of life.
- We cannot overcome this gap on our own: it is not humanly possible to bridge it. God is infinite, and only a divine, supernatural act, one of infinite worth, could repair it.

- God becomes man to overcome sin: Jesus became the living sacrifice that the Old Testament sacrifices only foreshadowed. He took all our sins on himself, freely, to free us from sin. Because he was both human and divine, he was able to do it: as man he could stand in our place, and as God his offering had infinite worth (Catechism 613-616).
No one took Jesus' life from him; he laid it down freely (John 10:18). The cross is not a picture of an angry God, but of a love that would go all the way for us.
## He descended to the dead
In the Creed we say Jesus "descended into hell." This does not mean the hell of the damned. It means the realm of the dead, which the Hebrews called Sheol and the Greeks Hades (Catechism 633).

Before Christ, all who died, whether evil or good, were deprived of the vision of God, waiting for the Messiah. Jesus, his human soul still united to his divine Person, went down to them. He did not go to free the damned or destroy the hell of damnation, but to open heaven's gates to the just who had gone before him (Catechism 632-637). This descent brings the Gospel of salvation to its complete fulfillment. It is the last phase of Jesus' mission as Messiah: short in time, but vast in meaning. On Holy Saturday his saving work reached all people of all times and places. Everyone, from the beginning of creation to the end of time, is brought into this redemption (Catechism 633-634).
## He rose from the dead

On the third day Jesus rose, truly and bodily. The tomb was empty, and he ate and spoke with his disciples, who were willing to die rather than deny it. St. Paul says that if Christ has not been raised, our faith is in vain (1 Corinthians 15:14).

By his death Jesus frees us from sin; by his resurrection he opens for us the way to a new life in him, so that we may become sons and daughters of God and have eternal life (Catechism 654). Jesus has raised us up to a new life! He has also opened the doors to heaven: eternal life with God and with all who have gone before us.
## Sharing in his cross

Jesus invites us into his death and resurrection. We can unite our whole lives with his cross: our daily work, our joys and our sufferings (Catechism 618). The cross and resurrection are the centre of history, and they are meant to be the centre of each of our lives too.
We will all suffer in some way during our lives; no one can avoid it. So the question should not be "Will I suffer?" but rather "What will I do when I suffer?"
- True love is always sacrificial: it is selfless, and always focused on God and others.
- Living only for yourself shrinks you: you become selfish, in denial of your own mortality and your true purpose.
- Suffering can be offered: our pain becomes a chance to unite ourselves with the suffering of Jesus, and to offer it for others (Colossians 1:24). Catholics sometimes call this "offering it up."
## A prayer to Christ Crucified
Your handout ends with this prayer by St. Thérèse of Lisieux. You can find it in Pray, and in the prayers listed with this session, so you can read it, listen to it and learn it.
> In the evening of this life, I shall appear before you with empty hands, for I do not ask you, Lord, to count my works. — St. Thérèse of Lisieux

St. Thérèse loved this image of empty hands. We come to the cross with nothing of our own to boast of, and there the empty are filled: Christ's hands, emptied for us, pour out mercy, and our hands, emptied for him and for others, are filled with his love.

deeper.title: The Triduum: three days at the heart of the year
deeper.text:
The Paschal Mystery is celebrated every Sunday, and above all in the Easter Triduum, the three holiest days of the Church year.

- Holy Thursday: the Mass of the Lord's Supper, when Jesus gives us the Eucharist and the priesthood, and washes his disciples' feet.

- Good Friday: the Celebration of the Lord's Passion. There is no Mass; we venerate the cross.

- Holy Saturday and the Easter Vigil: the Church waits at the tomb, then lights the new fire and sings the Exsultet. At the Vigil, those finishing RCIA are baptized, confirmed and receive their First Communion.

The Paschal Mystery is where your own journey is heading.

sessions.reflection: What is one suffering, big or small, that you are carrying now? Try offering it to Jesus this week, for someone you love. What changes when you do?

sessions.title: The Holy Spirit and the life of grace
sessions.summary: The Holy Spirit is God's own life poured into our hearts. Grace is that life at work in us, making us God's children.

sources.title: Galatians 5:16-26, the fruit of the Spirit

sessions.ref: Symbolon Part 1: Knowing the Faith · Session 7
lesson: Jesus promised his friends that he would not leave them orphans. Fifty days after Easter, at Pentecost, the Holy Spirit came upon the apostles like wind and tongues of fire, and the frightened disciples became bold witnesses (Acts 2).
## Who the Holy Spirit is

The Holy Spirit is not a force or a feeling. He is the third Person of the Holy Trinity, truly God with the Father and the Son. In the Creed we call him "the Lord, the giver of life" (Catechism 683-686).

Scripture uses images to help us picture him: water that cleanses and refreshes, fire that warms and purifies, wind and breath that give life, a dove of peace, and the anointing oil that marks someone as chosen (Catechism 694-701).
## What grace is
Grace is a free gift: God's own life shared with us. It is not something we earn. It heals us from sin and makes us sons and daughters of God, able to share his life (Catechism 1996-1999).
- Sanctifying grace: the lasting gift that makes our soul holy and pleasing to God. We first receive it in Baptism.
- Actual grace: God's help in a particular moment, nudging us to choose the good, to pray or to forgive.
Mortal sin drives sanctifying grace out of the soul. God restores it through the sacrament of Penance (Catechism 1861).
## The gifts and fruits of the Spirit
The Holy Spirit gives seven gifts that make us ready to follow his lead: wisdom, understanding, counsel, fortitude, knowledge, piety and fear of the Lord (Isaiah 11:2-3; Catechism 1831).

When we let him work in us, his fruits show in our lives: charity, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, generosity, gentleness, faithfulness, modesty, self-control and chastity (Galatians 5:22-23; Catechism 1832).
## Living by the Spirit
> The charity of God is poured forth in our hearts, by the Holy Ghost, who is given to us. — Romans 5:5, Douay-Rheims
The Spirit prays in us when we do not know how to pray (Romans 8:26). A simple way to begin each day is to say: "Come, Holy Spirit."
sessions.reflection: Which fruit of the Spirit would you most like to grow in your life this week? Ask the Holy Spirit for it each morning.

sessions.title: Why do I need the Church?
sessions.summary: Jesus founded the Church as his Body and his family. Through her he gives us his word, his sacraments and each other.
sessions.ref: Symbolon Part 1: Knowing the Faith · Session 8
lesson: Many people say, "I believe in Jesus, but I don't need the Church." The Catholic answer is that Jesus himself founded the Church, and that we meet him in her.
## Jesus founded the Church

Jesus chose twelve apostles, put Peter at their head, and gave him the keys of the kingdom (Matthew 16:18-19). He gave them his authority to teach, to forgive sins and to celebrate the Eucharist, and he sent them to all nations (Catechism 763-766).
The Church was born from the pierced side of Christ on the Cross, and she was shown to the world at Pentecost (Catechism 766-767).
## Images of the Church
- The Body of Christ: Christ is the head and we are the members. Each member has a part to play (1 Corinthians 12; Catechism 787-795).
- The Bride of Christ: Jesus loves the Church as a husband loves his wife, and gave himself up for her (Ephesians 5:25-27; Catechism 796).
- The People of God and the family of God: we become God's children together, not alone (Catechism 781-786).
- The Temple of the Holy Spirit: the Spirit lives in the Church and gives her life (Catechism 797-798).
## Four marks
In the Creed we say the Church is one, holy, catholic and apostolic (Catechism 811).
- One: one Lord, one faith, one Baptism, gathered around the Eucharist and the successor of Peter.
- Holy: not because her members never sin, but because Christ makes her holy and gives her every means of holiness.
- Catholic: universal. She has the fullness of the faith and is sent to every people in every age.
- Apostolic: built on the apostles, and still led by their successors, the bishops in communion with the pope.
## Why I need her

The Church gives us the Scriptures, the sacraments, the teaching that keeps the faith safe, and brothers and sisters to walk with. Faith is personal, but it is never private: we believe together (Catechism 166-169).
> He cannot have God for his father, who has not the Church for his mother. — St. Cyprian of Carthage
sessions.reflection: Who in your parish has helped you on your journey so far? Thank God for them, and think of one way you could help someone else there.

sessions.title: Mary and the saints
sessions.summary: Mary is the Mother of God and our mother. The saints are our family in heaven, praying for us.

sources.title: Luke 1:26-56, the Annunciation and the Magnificat
Catechism 484-511, 946-975: Mary and the communion of saints

sessions.ref: Symbolon Part 1: Knowing the Faith · Session 9
lesson: Catholics love Mary and the saints because they lead us to Jesus. We worship God alone; we honour Mary and the saints as his greatest works and as our family.
## Mary, Mother of God
Because her Son Jesus is one divine Person, Mary is truly the Mother of God, Theotokos (Catechism 495). This title is really a statement about who Jesus is.

At the Annunciation she said yes to God: "Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it done to me according to thy word" (Luke 1:38, Douay-Rheims). She is the model of faith for every Christian (Catechism 148, 967).
## What the Church believes about Mary
- Immaculate Conception: from the first moment of her life, Mary was kept free from original sin, by the grace of her Son (Catechism 490-493).
- Ever-virgin: Mary remained a virgin before, during and after the birth of Jesus (Catechism 496-507).
- Assumption: at the end of her life, Mary was taken body and soul into heavenly glory (Catechism 966).
- Mother of the Church: from the Cross, Jesus gave her to the beloved disciple, and to all of us, as our mother (John 19:26-27; Catechism 963-970).
## The communion of saints
The Church is one family in three places: those of us on earth, those being purified in purgatory, and the saints in heaven. Death does not break this family (Catechism 946-962).
Just as you can ask a friend to pray for you, you can ask the saints. They are alive in God and close to him, and their prayer is powerful (James 5:16; Catechism 956).
Each of us is called to be a saint. Canonized saints are those the Church declares are surely in heaven, and they show us that holiness is possible in every kind of life.
## Praying with Mary
The Hail Mary is made almost entirely of words from Scripture: the angel's greeting and Elizabeth's blessing (Luke 1:28, 42). The Rosary walks through the life of Jesus with Mary at our side.
sessions.reflection: Choose a saint to get to know this week, perhaps the one you picked in the app. Ask them to pray for you.

sessions.title: The last things
sessions.summary: Death, judgment, heaven, hell and purgatory: what the Church teaches about the end, and why it gives us hope.

sources.title: 1 Corinthians 15:35-58, the resurrection of the body
Catechism 988-1060: the resurrection of the body and life everlasting

sessions.ref: Symbolon Part 1: Knowing the Faith · Session 10
lesson: Everyone will die. The Christian faith does not avoid this fact; it faces it with hope, because Jesus has risen and opened the way to eternal life. These truths are called the last things.
## Death

Death is the end of our life on earth and of our time to choose for or against God. For a Christian it is not the end of life: "life is changed, not ended" (Preface for the Dead; Catechism 1005-1014).
## Judgment
- The particular judgment: right after death, each person's life is seen in the light of Christ, and our eternal destiny is decided (Catechism 1021-1022).
- The Last Judgment: at the end of time Christ will come again in glory, the dead will rise, and the whole truth of history will be revealed (Catechism 1038-1041).
Jesus told us what he will look for: "As long as you did it to one of these my least brethren, you did it to me" (Matthew 25:40, Douay-Rheims).
## Heaven

Heaven is perfect, endless happiness with God, the Blessed Virgin, the angels and all the saints. We will see God face to face. It is the fulfilment of every longing of the human heart (Catechism 1023-1029).
## Purgatory

Some die in God's friendship but are not yet fully purified. Purgatory is God's merciful cleansing before entering heaven. We can help them with our prayers, especially the Mass (Catechism 1030-1032).
## Hell

Hell is the state of definitive self-exclusion from God. God sends no one there against their will; it is the result of freely and finally refusing his love. The Church teaches this so that we will take our freedom seriously and turn to God now (Catechism 1033-1037).
## Living with the end in mind
These truths are not meant to frighten us but to wake us up. Every day is a chance to love God and our neighbour. And God's mercy is always open to anyone who turns to him.
sessions.reflection: If today were your last day, what would you want to put right? Pray for someone you love who has died.

sessions.title: Baptism and Confirmation
sessions.summary: Baptism makes us new creations and children of God. Confirmation seals us with the Holy Spirit and sends us out.

sources.title: Acts 8:14-17, the apostles lay hands on the baptized

sessions.ref: Symbolon Part 2: Living the Faith · Session 1
lesson: The sacraments are signs Jesus gave us that really do what they show. Through them he touches our lives with his grace (Catechism 1131). Baptism, Confirmation and the Eucharist are the three sacraments of initiation. They make us full members of the Church (Catechism 1212).
## Baptism

Baptism is the doorway to the Christian life. Water is poured, or we are immersed, with the words "I baptize you in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit" (Catechism 1239-1240).
- It washes away original sin and all personal sins (Catechism 1263).
- It makes us adopted children of God and members of the Body of Christ, the Church (Catechism 1265-1267).
- It marks the soul with a seal that can never be erased, so it is given only once (Catechism 1272).
The baptismal signs each have a meaning: the water of new life, the white garment of a new creation, and the candle lit from the Easter candle, because Christ is now our light (Catechism 1241-1243).
## Confirmation
Confirmation completes Baptism. The bishop or priest lays hands on us and anoints our forehead with sacred chrism, saying, "Be sealed with the Gift of the Holy Spirit" (Catechism 1300).
- It pours out the Holy Spirit as at Pentecost (Catechism 1302).
- It roots us more deeply as God's children, unites us more firmly to Christ and strengthens us to witness to him (Catechism 1303).
- Like Baptism, it marks us with a permanent seal and is received only once (Catechism 1304).
## For you at Easter

Adults who join the Church at the Easter Vigil receive all three sacraments of initiation in one night: Baptism (or, for those already baptized, reception into full communion), Confirmation, and First Communion. You will choose a Confirmation name, often a saint you want to imitate.
sessions.reflection: Think about the saint whose name you might take at Confirmation. What about their life draws you?

sessions.title: The Eucharist: source and summit
sessions.summary: In the Eucharist Jesus gives us himself: his Body and Blood, soul and divinity, under the appearance of bread and wine.
sessions.ref: Symbolon Part 2: Living the Faith · Session 2
lesson: The Church calls the Eucharist "the source and summit of the Christian life" (Catechism 1324). Every other sacrament and all the Church's work lead to it and flow from it, because the Eucharist is Jesus himself.
## Jesus promised it

After feeding five thousand people, Jesus said: "I am the living bread which came down from heaven. If any man eat of this bread, he shall live for ever" (John 6:51, Douay-Rheims). Many followers left because the teaching was hard, but Jesus did not soften it (John 6:60-69).
## Jesus gave it

At the Last Supper he took bread and said, "This is my body," and took the cup and said, "This is my blood of the new testament" (Matthew 26:26-28). He told the apostles, "Do this in commemoration of me" (Luke 22:19).
## Truly present

At Mass, by the words of Christ spoken by the priest and the power of the Holy Spirit, the bread and wine become the Body and Blood of Christ. They still look and taste like bread and wine, but their reality has changed. The Church calls this transubstantiation (Catechism 1373-1377).

Jesus is present whole and entire, Body, Blood, soul and divinity, in each part of the consecrated host and in the cup (Catechism 1374, 1377). That is why we kneel, genuflect to the tabernacle, and keep silence in church.
## A sacrifice and a meal
- A sacrifice: the Mass makes present the one sacrifice of Christ on the Cross. It is not repeated, but offered again in an unbloody way (Catechism 1366-1367).
- A meal: Jesus feeds us with himself, uniting us to him and to each other (Catechism 1391-1396).
## Receiving well

Catholics prepare to receive Communion by being in a state of grace (going to Confession first after a serious sin) and fasting for one hour beforehand (Catechism 1385-1387). Until your First Communion at Easter you can come forward for a blessing or make a spiritual communion from your seat.
sessions.reflection: Spend a few quiet minutes before the tabernacle this week. Tell Jesus what you are looking forward to about your First Communion.

sessions.title: A walk through the Mass
sessions.summary: The Mass has two main parts: the Liturgy of the Word, where God speaks to us, and the Liturgy of the Eucharist, where Jesus gives himself.

sources.title: Catechism 1345-1355: the celebration of the Eucharist

sessions.ref: Symbolon Part 2: Living the Faith · Session 3
lesson: The Mass follows the same pattern as the road to Emmaus: Jesus explained the Scriptures to the two disciples, and then they recognized him in the breaking of the bread (Luke 24:13-35; Catechism 1346-1347). The app's Mass guide under Learn walks through every step.
## Introductory Rites

We make the Sign of the Cross, the priest greets us, and we ask God's mercy in the Penitential Act ("Lord, have mercy"). On Sundays outside Advent and Lent we sing the Gloria, and the priest says the Opening Prayer (Collect).
## Liturgy of the Word
- First Reading: usually from the Old Testament.
- Responsorial Psalm: a sung or spoken prayer from the Psalms.
- Second Reading: on Sundays, from the letters of the New Testament.
- Gospel: we stand, because Christ himself speaks. The Alleluia greets it (except in Lent).
- Homily, Creed and Prayer of the Faithful: the priest explains the readings, we profess our faith, and we pray for the Church and the world.
## Liturgy of the Eucharist
- Preparation of the gifts: bread and wine are brought to the altar.
- Eucharistic Prayer: the heart of the Mass. It includes the Holy, Holy, Holy, the words of consecration, and the Great Amen. Most people kneel.
- Communion Rite: the Our Father, the sign of peace, the Lamb of God, and Holy Communion.
## Concluding Rites
The priest blesses us and sends us out: "Go forth, the Mass is ended," or "Go in peace." The word Mass comes from this sending: we carry Christ into the week (Catechism 1332).
## Taking part
Taking part does not mean doing everything perfectly. Listen, sing, say the responses, and offer your own week to God with the bread and wine at the altar.
sessions.reflection: Next Sunday, pay attention to one part of the Mass you usually rush past. What did you notice?

sessions.title: Penance and Anointing of the Sick
sessions.summary: Jesus heals us through two sacraments: Penance (Confession) forgives our sins, and the Anointing of the Sick strengthens the seriously ill.
sessions.ref: Symbolon Part 2: Living the Faith · Session 4
lesson: Even after Baptism we still sin. Jesus knew this, so he gave us two sacraments of healing (Catechism 1420-1421).
## Jesus forgives through the Church

On Easter evening Jesus breathed on the apostles and said: "Receive ye the Holy Ghost. Whose sins you shall forgive, they are forgiven them" (John 20:22-23, Douay-Rheims). Priests share this power from the apostles (Catechism 1441-1445).
## The parts of Confession
- Contrition: being truly sorry for our sins, out of love for God or fear of losing him, and resolving not to sin again (Catechism 1451-1454).
- Confession: telling our sins to the priest, especially every serious (mortal) sin we remember (Catechism 1455-1458).
- Absolution: the priest, acting in the person of Christ, forgives our sins (Catechism 1449).
- Penance: a prayer or action to help repair the harm and heal our hearts (Catechism 1459-1460).
The priest can never reveal what he hears. This is called the seal of confession, and it has no exceptions (Catechism 1467).
There is a step-by-step Confession guide and an Act of Contrition in the Pray tab. People already baptized in another church usually make their first Confession before Easter.
## Anointing of the Sick

This sacrament is for anyone seriously ill, facing major surgery, or weakened by old age, not only for the dying (Catechism 1514-1515). The priest lays hands on the sick person and anoints their forehead and hands with blessed oil (James 5:14-15).
It gives strength, peace and courage, unites the sick person's suffering with Christ's, forgives sins, and sometimes brings bodily healing if that is good for the soul (Catechism 1520-1523).
sessions.reflection: Look at the examination of conscience in the app. What is one thing you would like Jesus to heal in you?

sessions.title: Matrimony and Holy Orders
sessions.summary: Matrimony and Holy Orders are sacraments of service: they give grace to build up the Church through a life given for others.

sources.title: Genesis 2:18-24, the two become one flesh

sessions.ref: Symbolon Part 2: Living the Faith · Session 5
lesson: Two sacraments are directed to the salvation of others: Holy Orders and Matrimony. They give a special mission in the Church and the grace to live it (Catechism 1534-1535).
## Matrimony

In marriage a man and a woman give themselves to each other for their whole lives, open to children. Between baptized people this covenant is a sacrament: a sign of Christ's love for his Church (Ephesians 5:31-32; Catechism 1601).
- The couple themselves are the ministers: they give the sacrament to each other by their free consent, with the priest or deacon as the Church's witness (Catechism 1623, 1630).
- Marriage is one (faithful), lasting until death, and open to life (Catechism 1643-1654).
- The family is a "domestic church," the first place where children learn to pray and believe (Catechism 1655-1658).
If you are already married, or were married before, talk with your RCIA leader or priest. The parish helps each couple check their situation before Easter.
## Holy Orders
Holy Orders is the sacrament through which the mission Christ gave the apostles continues in the Church. It has three degrees (Catechism 1536, 1554):
- Bishops: successors of the apostles, with the fullness of the sacrament.
- Priests: co-workers of the bishops, who celebrate the sacraments, preach and lead parishes.
- Deacons: ordained for service, who baptize, preach, witness marriages and serve the poor.
A priest acts "in the person of Christ the Head" when he celebrates the sacraments (Catechism 1548). Like Baptism and Confirmation, Holy Orders leaves a permanent mark.
## Every vocation
Every Christian has a vocation, a call from God. Whether married, ordained, in religious life or single, each of us is called to give our life in love.
sessions.reflection: Pray this week for a married couple you admire, and for your parish priest.

sessions.title: A Catholic moral vision
sessions.summary: God's commandments are not a cage but a path to happiness. Virtue and grace make that path possible.

sources.title: Matthew 5-7, the Sermon on the Mount

sessions.ref: Symbolon Part 2: Living the Faith · Session 6
lesson: Every person wants to be happy. The Catholic moral life starts there: God made us for happiness, and he shows us the way to it (Catechism 1718-1719).
## The Beatitudes

Jesus began his Sermon on the Mount with the Beatitudes: "Blessed are the poor in spirit… blessed are the meek… blessed are the merciful…" (Matthew 5:3-12). They describe the face of Jesus himself and the true happiness he offers (Catechism 1716-1717).
## Freedom and conscience
- Freedom: real freedom is not doing whatever we feel like, but being able to choose the good. The more we do good, the freer we become (Catechism 1731-1733).
- Conscience: the inner voice that tells us to do good and avoid evil. It must be formed by God's word and the Church's teaching, and then we must follow it (Catechism 1776-1785).
## The Ten Commandments

The first three are about loving God; the other seven are about loving our neighbour (Catechism 2067). Jesus summed them up in two great commandments: love God with all your heart, and love your neighbour as yourself (Matthew 22:37-40).
- I am the Lord your God: you shall not have strange gods before me.
- You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain.
- Remember to keep holy the Lord's Day.
- Honour your father and your mother.
- You shall not kill.
- You shall not commit adultery.
- You shall not steal.
- You shall not bear false witness against your neighbour.
- You shall not covet your neighbour's wife.
- You shall not covet your neighbour's goods.
## Virtues
A virtue is a firm habit of doing good (Catechism 1803).
- The cardinal virtues, which we grow in by practice: prudence, justice, fortitude and temperance (Catechism 1805-1809).
- The theological virtues, gifts God pours into us: faith, hope and charity. The greatest of these is charity (1 Corinthians 13:13; Catechism 1812-1829).
## Sin and mercy

Sin is a failure to love God and neighbour. Mortal sin is a grave matter done with full knowledge and deliberate consent; it cuts us off from God's grace until we repent. Venial sin weakens our love but does not break it (Catechism 1854-1863). God's mercy is always greater than our sin.
sessions.reflection: Which of the Beatitudes speaks to you most right now? Which virtue would you like to grow in?

sessions.title: A love that lasts: discovering authentic love
sessions.summary: Real love is not just a feeling. It is a gift of self, willing the good of the other, and it comes from God who is love.
sessions.ref: Symbolon Part 2: Living the Faith · Session 7
lesson: The word love is used for everything from pizza to marriage. The Church helps us see what real love is, because we were made in the image of God, and "God is love" (1 John 4:8).
## Love is a gift of self

Love is more than a feeling, though feelings are good. To love is to will the good of another and to give ourselves for them (Catechism 1766). Jesus showed what that means: "Greater love than this no man hath, that a man lay down his life for his friends" (John 15:13, Douay-Rheims).
## Using versus loving

The opposite of love is not only hate; it is also using. Using someone means treating them as a means to get something for ourselves. Love sees each person as someone willed by God for their own sake, never as an object (Catechism 2284, 2357-2359).
## What love looks like

St. Paul describes it: love is patient and kind; it is not jealous, proud or rude; it does not seek its own interests; it bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things (1 Corinthians 13:4-7).
## Made for communion

God created us male and female, equal in dignity and made for each other (Genesis 1:27; Catechism 369-372). Our whole person, body and soul, is made for communion with God and with others. That is why love involves the body as well as the heart.
## Chastity is for everyone

Chastity is the virtue that brings our desires into harmony with real love, so that we can give ourselves freely and not be ruled by our urges. Every Christian is called to it, in a way that fits their state of life: married, single, or consecrated (Catechism 2337-2349).
## Where love comes from
We can only love this way with God's help. "We love, because he first loved us" (1 John 4:19). Prayer and the sacraments are where we receive the love we are meant to give away.
sessions.reflection: Think of someone who has loved you with a self-giving love. How can you love one person like that this week?

sessions.title: A love that lasts: God's plan for sexuality
sessions.summary: Sexuality is a gift from God, meant to express the total, faithful and fruitful love of husband and wife.

sources.title: Genesis 1:26-31 and 2:18-25, male and female he created them
1 Corinthians 6:12-20, your body is a temple

sessions.ref: Symbolon Part 2: Living the Faith · Session 8
lesson: The Church's teaching on sexuality is often heard only as a list of rules. It is really a big yes: a yes to the dignity of the body, to faithful love, and to the gift of children.
## The body speaks
We do not just have bodies; we are bodies and souls together. The body is good, created by God and redeemed by Christ, and it is a temple of the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 6:19-20; Catechism 364).

Pope St. John Paul II taught that the body has a language. Sexual union says, with the body, "I give myself to you completely, for always." It speaks the truth only within marriage, where that promise has actually been made (Catechism 2360-2363).
## God's plan for married love
In marriage, sexual love has two inseparable purposes (Catechism 2366-2369):
- Unitive: it unites husband and wife ever more deeply in love.
- Procreative: it is open to new life, so that husband and wife share in God's work of creation.

Married couples may use natural methods to space births for serious reasons, respecting both purposes; the Church teaches that contraception separates them (Catechism 2370). Parishes offer courses in natural family planning.
## Mercy for everyone

Many people have experiences or choices in their past that do not match this vision. The Church does not reject anyone. Christ's mercy in the sacrament of Penance is a new beginning, and every person is called to chastity with the help of grace (Catechism 2348-2350). Every person, whatever their situation, is to be treated with respect and love (Catechism 2358).
## A vision worth living
This teaching protects love from being used and cheapened. It points to the greatest love of all: Christ's love for his Church, total, faithful and life-giving (Ephesians 5:25).
sessions.reflection: What part of this teaching do you find beautiful? What part do you have questions about? Bring your questions to your RCIA leader.

sessions.title: Catholic social teaching: a civilization of love
sessions.summary: Catholic social teaching shows how to build a society of justice and love, with special care for the poor.

sources.title: Matthew 25:31-46, I was hungry and you gave me food
Compendium of the Social Doctrine of the Church

sessions.ref: Symbolon Part 2: Living the Faith · Session 9
lesson: Faith is never only between me and God. Jesus identified himself with the hungry, the stranger, the sick and the prisoner (Matthew 25:35-40). The Church's social teaching applies the Gospel to life in society.
## Key principles
- The common good: the conditions that let every person and group flourish. Everyone shares responsibility for it (Catechism 1905-1912).
- Solidarity: we are one human family. We are responsible for each other, especially across borders and between rich and poor (Catechism 1939-1942).

- Subsidiarity: problems should be handled at the closest level that can handle them well, starting with the family and local community, with larger bodies helping rather than taking over (Catechism 1883-1885).
- The preferential option for the poor: in every decision, ask how it affects the poorest and most vulnerable (Catechism 2443-2449).
- The dignity of work: work is a way to share in God's creation. Workers have a right to fair wages and safe conditions (Catechism 2427-2436).
- Care for creation: the earth is a gift entrusted to us for all generations (Catechism 2415-2418).
## Works of mercy
The Church lists concrete ways to love (Catechism 2447):
- Corporal: feed the hungry, give drink to the thirsty, clothe the naked, shelter the homeless, visit the sick, visit the imprisoned, bury the dead.
- Spiritual: instruct the ignorant, counsel the doubtful, admonish sinners, bear wrongs patiently, forgive offences willingly, comfort the afflicted, pray for the living and the dead.
## A civilization of love

Popes have called Christians to build "a civilization of love." It starts small: in families, in the parish, at work. Many parishes in Canada have a St. Vincent de Paul Society or a food bank where new Catholics can serve.
sessions.reflection: Choose one work of mercy to do this week, and do it quietly, for Jesus.

sessions.title: Catholic social teaching: the dignity of every person
sessions.summary: Every human life is sacred, from conception to natural death, because each person is made in the image of God.

sources.title: Genesis 1:26-31, in the image of God

sessions.ref: Symbolon Part 2: Living the Faith · Session 10
lesson: The foundation of all Catholic social teaching is the dignity of the human person. Every human being is made in the image and likeness of God (Genesis 1:27) and is loved by him for their own sake (Catechism 356-357, 1700).
## Life is sacred
Human life is sacred from the moment of conception until natural death, because God alone is its Lord (Catechism 2258). That is why the Church defends life at every stage:
- The unborn: the Church teaches that direct abortion is gravely wrong, and she surrounds women in difficult pregnancies with practical help and mercy (Catechism 2270-2275).

- The sick, disabled and elderly: their lives have the same worth. Euthanasia and assisted suicide are contrary to the dignity of the person; good palliative care is a work of love (Catechism 2276-2283).
- Every person: the Church also works against violence, poverty, racism, human trafficking and the abuse of migrants and refugees, all of which wound human dignity (Catechism 2284-2317).
## Rights and duties

Because every person has dignity, every person has rights: to life, to food and shelter, to religious freedom, to work, to education. With rights come duties to respect the rights of others (Catechism 1929-1933).
## Healing and hope

Many people carry wounds connected to these questions, such as a past abortion. God's mercy is greater than any sin. In Canada, Rachel's Vineyard and parish priests offer confidential help and healing.
## Seeing as God sees
> As long as you did it to one of these my least brethren, you did it to me. — Matthew 25:40, Douay-Rheims
Mother Teresa saw Jesus in the poorest of the poor. The challenge for each of us is to see every person, especially the one who is easy to overlook, as someone God has willed and loves.
sessions.reflection: Who is someone easy to overlook in your daily life? How could you show them their dignity this week?

sessions.title: Lent: prayer, fasting, almsgiving
sessions.summary: Lent is forty days of preparing for Easter through prayer, fasting and almsgiving. For you it is the final retreat before the sacraments.
lesson: Lent begins on Ash Wednesday and lasts forty days, recalling Jesus' forty days of fasting in the desert (Matthew 4:1-11). For the whole Church it is a time of conversion; for the elect, those preparing for Baptism, it is the final and most intense stage of preparation (Catechism 540, 1438).
## Ash Wednesday

Ashes are placed on our foreheads with the words "Repent, and believe in the Gospel" or "Remember that you are dust, and to dust you shall return." Anyone may receive ashes, including those not yet baptized.
## Three practices
Jesus speaks of all three in the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 6:1-18):
- Prayer: turning back to God. Add something: a daily Gospel reading, the Stations of the Cross on Fridays, or a few quiet minutes in church.

- Fasting: letting go of food or comforts so that we hunger for God. Catholics aged 18 to 59 fast on Ash Wednesday and Good Friday (one full meal and two small ones), and those 14 and older abstain from meat on those days and on Fridays of Lent.
- Almsgiving: giving to those in need, with money, time or attention. What we save by fasting can go to the poor; in Canada many parishes support Development and Peace's Share Lent.
## Why give things up?
Lent is not about proving how strong we are. Small sacrifices make room in our hearts, help us notice our attachments, and unite us with Jesus who gave everything for us.
## For the elect

On the first Sunday of Lent the elect usually celebrate the Rite of Election with the bishop. Then come the scrutinies and the presentations of the Creed and the Lord's Prayer. Let your whole parish pray for you, and pray for each other.
sessions.reflection: Choose one practice of prayer, one of fasting and one of almsgiving for this Lent. Write them in your journal so you can look back at Easter.

sessions.title: The scrutinies: turning toward Christ
sessions.summary: On the third, fourth and fifth Sundays of Lent the parish prays over the elect, asking God to heal what is weak and strengthen what is good.

sources.title: John 4:5-42, the woman at the well

lesson: The scrutinies are prayers of healing and strength for the elect, celebrated at Mass on the third, fourth and fifth Sundays of Lent. "Scrutiny" sounds like an exam, but it is not a test of you. It is God looking into the heart with love, to uncover and heal whatever is weak or sinful, and to strengthen all that is good.
## Three Gospels, three encounters
The readings come from Year A, the oldest Gospels the Church has used with those preparing for Baptism:
- First scrutiny, the woman at the well (John 4:5-42): Jesus offers living water to someone thirsty for more. He knows everything about her and still offers her life.
- Second scrutiny, the man born blind (John 9:1-41): Jesus is the light of the world. He opens eyes, and the man comes to faith step by step.
- Third scrutiny, the raising of Lazarus (John 11:1-45): Jesus is the resurrection and the life. He calls us out of every tomb.
## What happens

After the homily the elect come forward, often with their godparents or sponsors, who place a hand on their shoulder. The parish prays for them. The priest prays a prayer of exorcism, asking God to free them from the power of evil, and lays hands on them in silence.
An exorcism here is not a dramatic movie scene. It is a quiet prayer of the whole Church, asking Christ to set someone free (Catechism 1237).
## Preparing your heart
Before each scrutiny, read the Gospel and ask: What thirst do I bring to Jesus? Where am I still blind? What tomb do I need him to call me out of?
sessions.reflection: Which of the three Gospel stories speaks most to where you are now? Write a short prayer to Jesus about it.

sessions.title: The Creed is handed on to you
sessions.summary: The Church hands on to you her profession of faith, the Creed, so that you can make it your own at Baptism.
lesson: During Lent the Church gives the elect two treasures: the Creed and the Lord's Prayer. These are called the Presentations. In the early Church, the elect learned the Creed by heart and "gave it back" by reciting it before their Baptism.
## What a creed is

A creed is a summary of the faith. The word comes from the Latin credo, "I believe." Creeds are also called symbols, from a Greek word for a token that proves you belong. That is where the name Symbolon comes from (Catechism 185-188).
## Two creeds
- The Apostles' Creed: the ancient baptismal creed of the Church in Rome (Catechism 194).
- The Nicene Creed: from the Councils of Nicaea (325) and Constantinople (381), said at Sunday Mass (Catechism 195).
## Its shape
The Creed has three parts, one for each Person of the Trinity (Catechism 190):
- God the Father and creation.
- God the Son and our redemption: his birth, death, resurrection and return.
- God the Holy Spirit and our sanctification: the Church, the forgiveness of sins, the resurrection and eternal life.
Look back over your lessons: almost every one has explained a line of the Creed.
## Making it your own

At the Easter Vigil, before you are baptized, you will be asked: "Do you believe in God, the Father almighty…?" and you will answer, "I do." Learn the Apostles' Creed by heart this week. The app's Pray tab can read it aloud with you.
sessions.reflection: Which line of the Creed means the most to you right now? Which one do you still have questions about?

sessions.title: The Lord's Prayer is handed on to you
sessions.summary: The Church hands on to you the prayer Jesus himself taught, the Our Father, the summary of the whole Gospel.
lesson: When the disciples asked Jesus, "Lord, teach us to pray," he gave them the Our Father (Luke 11:1-4). The Church presents this prayer to the elect during Lent. After Baptism you will pray it as a child of God, calling him Father in a new way. Tertullian called it "the summary of the whole Gospel" (Catechism 2761).
## Our Father, who art in heaven
We call God Father because Jesus lets us share his own relationship with the Father. "Our" reminds us we never pray alone (Catechism 2779-2796).
## Seven petitions
The first three are about God, the last four about our needs (Catechism 2803-2806):
- Hallowed be thy name: may God's name be honoured as holy, in us and in the world.
- Thy kingdom come: may God's reign of love grow now and come in fullness when Christ returns.
- Thy will be done on earth as it is in heaven: may we want what God wants.
- Give us this day our daily bread: everything we need, and also the Bread of Life, the Eucharist.
- Forgive us our trespasses as we forgive those who trespass against us: God's mercy flows into a heart that also forgives.
- Lead us not into temptation: give us strength not to give in when we are tested.
- Deliver us from evil: free us from the evil one and all his works.
## Praying it slowly
Try praying the Our Father very slowly, one phrase per breath, stopping on the line that catches your heart. St. Teresa of Avila said a person could spend a whole hour on it.
sessions.reflection: Which line of the Our Father is hardest for you to pray honestly? Bring that to God this week.

sessions.title: Holy Week and the Easter Vigil
sessions.summary: Holy Week leads to the Easter Vigil, the night you receive the sacraments. Here is what to expect.

sources.title: John 13-20, from the Last Supper to the empty tomb

lesson: Holy Week is the most important week of the Church year. It walks with Jesus through his last days, his death and his resurrection (Catechism 1168-1169).
## Palm Sunday
We carry palms and remember Jesus entering Jerusalem as king, then hear the whole Passion read aloud.
## The Easter Triduum
The three days from Holy Thursday evening to Easter Sunday evening are one great celebration.

- Holy Thursday: the Mass of the Lord's Supper. Jesus gives us the Eucharist and the priesthood and washes his disciples' feet. Afterwards the Blessed Sacrament is carried to an altar of repose for quiet prayer.
- Good Friday: no Mass is celebrated. We hear the Passion, pray for the whole world, and come forward to venerate the Cross. It is a day of fasting.
- Holy Saturday: the Church waits in silence at the tomb. In many parishes the elect gather in the morning for prayer and the "Ephphatha" rite, opening their ears and mouths to the Gospel.
## The Easter Vigil
After dark, the Church celebrates the greatest night of the year (Catechism 1217):
- The Service of Light: a new fire is blessed and the Easter candle lit. Its light passes from candle to candle, and the Exsultet, the great Easter proclamation, is sung.
- The Liturgy of the Word: several readings tell the whole story of salvation, from creation to the Resurrection. The Gloria and the Alleluia return.
- Baptism and Confirmation: the elect renounce sin, profess faith, and are baptized and confirmed. Candidates already baptized make their profession of faith and are confirmed.
- The Eucharist: you receive Holy Communion for the first time.
## Practical tips

The Vigil can last two to three hours. Wear clothes that can get a little wet if you are being baptized by immersion, and ask your parish what to bring. Eat lightly before, rest during the day, and invite the people who love you.
sessions.reflection: Write a short letter to yourself to open on the night of the Easter Vigil. What do you hope for?

sessions.title: Living the sacraments
sessions.summary: Easter changed you. Mystagogy is the time to unpack what the sacraments did and to grow in your new life.

sources.title: Acts 2:42-47, the life of the first believers

lesson: The weeks after Easter are called mystagogy, from a Greek word meaning "being led into the mysteries." The early Church saved some explanations until after Baptism, because the sacraments are best understood once you have lived them.
## What changed
- In Baptism you became a new creation, a child of God, and a member of Christ's Body (2 Corinthians 5:17; Catechism 1265).
- In Confirmation the Holy Spirit sealed you and gave you his gifts for your mission (Catechism 1303).
- In the Eucharist you were united to Jesus, and you can now receive him every Sunday, even every day (Catechism 1391).
## Keeping the new life strong
- Sunday Mass: the heart of Catholic life, and an obligation every Sunday and holy day (Catechism 2180-2183).
- Confession: go regularly, not only when you have committed a serious sin. Many Catholics go once a month (Catechism 1458).
- Daily prayer: keep the habits you started in RCIA: morning offering, Scripture, evening examen.
- Community: stay connected with your sponsor and your RCIA group.
## The precepts of the Church

The Church gives five basic duties as a minimum: attend Mass on Sundays and holy days; confess serious sins at least once a year; receive Communion at least during the Easter season; observe the days of fasting and abstinence; and help provide for the needs of the Church (Catechism 2041-2043).
## Neophytes
For this first year you are called a neophyte, a "new plant." Expect ups and downs. Feelings fade, but grace remains. Keep showing up.
sessions.reflection: What surprised you about your first weeks as a Catholic? Which habit do you most want to keep?

sessions.title: Called and sent
sessions.summary: At Pentecost the Spirit sends the Church out on mission. Every Catholic has a part to play, starting in the parish.

sources.title: Catechism 849-856 and 897-913: mission and the laity

lesson: Fifty days after Easter, the Church celebrates Pentecost. The Holy Spirit came down on the apostles, and they went out to proclaim Jesus to every nation (Acts 2). Pentecost closes the Easter season and the RCIA journey, but it is really a beginning.
## Sent, not just saved

Jesus' last words to his disciples were a mission: "Going therefore, teach ye all nations; baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost" (Matthew 28:19, Douay-Rheims). Every baptized person shares in that mission (Catechism 849, 900).
## Your gifts

The Spirit gives each of us gifts for the good of others (1 Corinthians 12:4-7). Think about what you are good at and what you love: music, hospitality, teaching children, visiting the sick, practical help.
## Places to start in your parish
- Liturgy: reader (lector), greeter, choir, server.
- Faith formation: helping with children's catechism or with next year's RCIA group.
- Service: the St. Vincent de Paul Society, food bank, visiting seniors.
- Prayer: Eucharistic adoration, a Bible study, a prayer group.
## Witness
Most evangelization is simple: living with joy and telling people, when they ask, why you became Catholic. Your story of the road you walked is one of the most powerful things you can share.
## Like the Emmaus disciples

You began this journey with the two disciples on the road to Emmaus. After they recognized Jesus in the breaking of the bread, they got up that very hour and ran back to share the news (Luke 24:33-35). That is your story now too.
